verses.text: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD!
Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!
May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.

context.author: The title calls it “A song of ascents,” one of fifteen such psalms (120-134). They may have been sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the feasts; the Mishnah says the Levites sang them on the fifteen steps inside the Temple courts (Sukkah 5:4). This is the last of the fifteen.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship, and the nations called to join
context.setting: The last Song of Ascents is a short exchange in the Temple at night. Pilgrims, perhaps leaving after the feast, call to the Levites on duty: “Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who serve by night in the house of the LORD! Lift up your hands to the sanctuary and bless the LORD!” (vv.1-2). The priests answer with a blessing for the pilgrims: “May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion” (v.3).
context.custom: Levites kept watch in the Temple day and night (1 Chronicles 9:27, 33). Lifting the hands was the posture of prayer and blessing (Leviticus 9:22; 1 Timothy 2:8). The pilgrims who came “up” to Jerusalem in Psalm 120 now go home with God’s blessing.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 135 praises the LORD who chose Israel and is greater than all idols.
context.timelineBible: Anna the prophetess “never left the temple, but worshiped night and day” (Luke 2:37). Before His ascension, Jesus “lifted up His hands and blessed them” (Luke 24:50). Revelation pictures the redeemed serving God “day and night in His temple” (Revelation 7:15).

overview.summary: The last pilgrim song: worshipers call the Temple’s night servants to bless the LORD, and the priests bless them in return from Zion.
overview.settingLine: Night in the Temple, blessing given and received.

archaeology.t: The seven-branched lampstand carved on the Arch of Titus.
Silver scrolls with the priestly blessing.

overview.discussion: Blessing goes both ways: to God and from God (vv.1-3). Who could I bless today, and when will I take time to bless the LORD?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (all 150 in the app). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: Not named
overview.genre: Song of ascents; liturgy of blessing
